This initial size places neonates among the smallest of the chydorid cladocerans, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid population turnover over large investment per offspring. Upon release, these juveniles measure less than half the length they will eventually attain as fully grown adults, highlighting the substantial scope for somatic growth that defines their early development. The period immediately following release is one of intense morphological change, as the carapace begins to expand and the postabdomen takes on its characteristic form. Within the first two days post-release, the rate of length increase is notably high, a pattern observed in many cladoceran taxa. The precise length at this early stage is a critical baseline for constructing accurate growth models and has been used extensively in comparative studies of body size evolution across the Chydoridae. The progression from birth to this point represents a critical window during which resource acquisition must be maximized to fuel the impending reproductive effort. Any delay in reaching this length can significantly impact lifetime fecundity. These measurements provide a clear picture of the rapid pace of maturation in this species, a pace that is consistent with its role as a pioneer species in temporary aquatic habitats.

Adult females of Coronatella rectangula eventually achieve an ultimate total length of 0.0468 cm [Li = 0.0468 cm], a size at which somatic growth effectively ceases and resources are directed almost entirely toward reproduction. This asymptotic length is modest relative to many other cladocerans but is typical for the subfamily Aloninae. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of fully grown individuals is approximately 0.000011 grams [Wwi = approximately 0.000011 grams], a mass derived from morphometric measurements assuming a length of 0.047 cm, a height of 0.03 cm, and a width of 0.0100 cm. This minute mass places them among the lightest of freshwater microcrustaceans, a trait that facilitates efficient filter feeding on suspended algae and bacteria. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a typical allometric curve, with weight increasing roughly as the cube of length. Adult body size is a key determinant of fecundity, as larger females can accommodate more eggs within their brood chamber. The ultimate total length and its associated wet weight thus represent the culmination of the juvenile growth phase and the beginning of a dedicated reproductive period.

The combination of moderate clutch size and high frequency of reproduction is a classic r-selected strategy, enabling rapid population growth in ephemeral ponds and shallow lakes. Such a strategy is common among small-bodied cladocerans that face high levels of predation risk from insects and fish. The rapid cycling of generations and the ability to switch to resting egg production when conditions deteriorate are central to the ecological success of this species.

This duration encompasses the entire life cycle from embryonic development through senescence and natural death. The relatively brief lifespan means that a female can complete multiple reproductive events within a single season, maximizing her contribution to the next generation. Older individuals exhibit reduced brood sizes and longer interclutch intervals before eventually ceasing reproduction entirely. This timeline is consistent with the seasonal dynamics of temperate ponds, where populations must complete their life cycle before habitats dry up or freeze over in winter. The interplay between rapid development, early maturity, and high reproductive output allows Coronatella rectangula to thrive as a dominant member of the littoral zooplankton community.
